items.title: littleFedi
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
littleFedi is "A small ActivityPub server written in Go"

A few years ago I'd decided I wanted to "own my content" 🙄 so I ran an instance of Mastodon. Mastodon is overkill and I didn't enjoy it. Then, later, I installed an instance of Go2Social, which worked well. Trouble was, I was all-in with social media at the time and being on a single-user instance felt lonely...nothing useful in "local" or "trending". Discovery was difficult. It was just me and I didn't like it.

Fast forward to today, and things have changed. I've deleted all of my Meta-related accounts and LinkedIn. I thought about quitting Mastodon as well, but FOMO always gets the better of me.

Since I would rather not quit Mastodon completely, I figured I would try running a single-user instance again. Maybe the quiet would be good for me.

I'd seen @Stefano's posts about a new ActivityPub server he was working on and the timing of the first release couldn't be better, so I installed it today at Jack Baty Social.

It's running on my Hetzner VPS behind Caddy as a proxy. I love Caddy. Here's the entire Caddy config for the domain:

social.baty.net {
	encode gzip
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8081
}

I've just started poking around, but littleFedi seems like it's got a lot going for it. At first I wanted to use my root domain for my handle () but since I'd previously used that via Ghost, I ran into caching issues and didn't want to bother, so now I'm @jack@social.baty.net.

The big question is whether to migrate followers there, or start fresh and maybe just announce the move from my main @jbaty@social.lol account. I think I'll give it a minute before deciding.

littleFedi is a compelling new entry in the FediverseSpaceArena.

items.title: Friday, October 2, 2026
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content: Sal's follow-up to my post about ending my Linux experiment includes a note about Apple Messages. I can't believe I didn't mention that. One of the biggest drawbacks for me on Linux was not having easy access to Messages. (Nearly) everyone I correspond with uses Messages. I hate typing anything on my iPhone, so having to switch to my phone to text someone was no fun at all. And forget about sharing a funny meme or whatever. I could never get KDE Connect, LocalSend, and friends to work fast enough or consistently enough to make it worth it. It was one hurdle I was never able to clear when using Linux.

items.title: I am comfortable living in Linux, but...
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
After many failed attempts, I am finally comfortable doing all of my computing using Linux. In case you haven't heard, Linux is good now! And yet, I'm back on my Mac...for now.

The short version? It's the software. Linux is loaded with pretty good apps, many of them free. Thing is, nearly all of them also run on macOS. This means that on a Mac, I can use all the great macOS software, and most of the great apps I use on Linux..

I've spent the past year recreating the dozens of little workflows on Linux that I'd built for myself on the Mac. Some of them were easily portable, but many weren't. Some had no real replacements, so I had to give them up.

The things I like about Linux are abstract. The "I'm in complete control of my computing environment" kind of things. I miss that feeling on the Mac, especially when I can't launch an app that I downloaded or when I've had to dismiss the two thousandth permissions dialog that day. Also, I love the "This twelve-year-old ThinkPad still works great running Linux!"

What I don't miss are all the Linux distros. I mean, what an embarrassment of riches, right? Except my brain never stops thinking "What if I switched to...?" every other day. Half the time I actually have switched, with disastrous effects on my time. I don't enjoy the community bickering either. "Systemd sucks!" and so on. And there's still too much "Um, actually..." and "Why don't you just...?"

Overall, my year-long adventure with Linux was fun and successful. But I don't want to give up some of the Mac software I've used for years...sometimes years.

What might be the biggest draw of macOS for me is that I automatically get Emacs key bindings everywhere. I hadn't realized how much I relied on them until they were gone.

I'm sure I'll revisit this again at some point. I still have a couple of nice laptops running Linux, and I'll certainly pop them open occasionally, but for now, I'm going to live on my Mac.

I know some of you have been rooting for me to fully adopt Linux. Please don't be too disappointed. Everything with me is temporary :). At least I know I can switch completely to Linux if I want to. I'm just not ready.

items.title: A Swift wrapper for my little CMS
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
I didn't want the Baty.net Editor to be just another tab buried in my browser, so I had Claude make me a real Mac app out of it.

In a normal world, the only way I'd be able to split a website into its own app would be "Add to Dock" via Safari. That would work, but it would mean that running the local Node server for Eleventy was a separate step from the app. It would also only have Safari's default menus.

I wanted something nicer, so I had Claude build me a Swift wrapper. I suppose I could have used something like Electron, but my Mac Mini only has 16 GB of memory, so Electron would be too heavy.

It took Claude Code 15 minutes to wrap the thing, create the app, add an icon, write the readme, and commit all of it. What a world.

When I launch the app, it starts the server automatically. Also, there are actual menus.

It's currently using only 99 MB of memory. This stuff makes me a little giddy.

items.title: Monday, September 28, 2026
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
My little SSG CMS has changed the way I feel about writing on this blog. I'm sure it's a reaction to Text File Fatigue. I've hit a wall with looking at everything I read and write via Emacs. I'm bored with it, so writing in this clean, simple little web UI is refreshing.

Speaking of subscriptions, subscription fatigue has a been a thing with me for a while. My rule now is that unless you're providing me with infrastructure, storage, or some other service that has ongoing costs for you, I'm not paying a subscription fee. An app that I download once and then just does what it does, all by itself, should not require a monthly payment from me. LLMs have gotten so good at creating useful, personal tools that the first thing I think when I see that an app has an unnecessary subscription is, "I guess I'll just make my own."

items.title: Sunday, September 27, 2026

items.content: I'm back on my Mac and all-in with Bear again right now. Working on an Alfred workflow for daily notes and logging. So refreshing!

items.title: Baty.net Editor
items.author: Jack Baty
items.content:
Usually, when I grow tired of editing blog posts using Markdown files in Emacs or whatever, I create a new blog using Ghost or something like it. This time, I did something different.

Sometimes I just want a nice, easy, CMS for blogging. Emacs and a few lisp function are not that, so I asked Claude Code to make me a web app.

At 7:00 am I sent the following to Claude:

My blog at baty.net is managed locally using Eleventy. I would like to build a local web app that allows me to create new content. It should have "New Post", "New Journal", "New Page", and "New Note" options. The editor should handle Markdown, but it doesn't necessarily have to be "WYSIWYG" . There's should be a way to start the local server ("just serve") and deploy ("just deploy"). The blog is currently in ~/sites/baty.net.

I walked away and made breakfast.

At 7:27 am Claude said this:

I used it to write a test post, and it worked, first try. The app needed no edits. I later added a few niceties, but all-in this first version took less than an hour to build and I'm using it to write this post.
